passage:
Dear Jasleen,

I keep replaying the wedding. When I said I disagreed with the government on one policy, a distant relative called me brainwashed and anti-national, loudly, with people listening. My cheeks burned. I wanted to fire back with everything I had.

Instead I said, "I see it differently, and I care about this country as much as you do. I'm going to get some tea." And I went. That was all. Nobody won.

I've been asking myself why it hurt so much. I think it's being turned into a label, when I'm a person with a view. But I feel calm now, calmer than I would have if I had stayed and argued.

Thank you for always letting me say things half-formed.

Alka

qa.q: What labels did the relative use for Alka?
qa.a: The relative called Alka brainwashed and anti-national.

qa.q: How did Alka feel, and how did Alka handle it?
qa.a: Alka felt stung, with burning cheeks and an urge to fire back, but answered briefly and walked away to get tea.

qa.q: What could Alka do if the relative brings it up again?
qa.a: State the view briefly, decline to be defined by the label, and end the conversation calmly.

qa.q: How might Jasleen feel on reading this letter?
qa.a: Trusted, since Alka thanks Jasleen for always letting half-formed thoughts be said.

grounding: Alka is dismissed as brainwashed and anti-national, states a view briefly, ends the talk calmly and refuses to be defined by the label.

passage:
Gurpreet: saw your post on the farm laws thing
Gurpreet: honestly, you sound brainwashed
Gurpreet: or anti-national, not sure which
Arnab: That hurt to read.
Arnab: I've been writing a reply for twenty minutes.
Arnab: Here's the short version: I think the farmers weren't consulted enough. That's my view.
Gurpreet: that's exactly what the brainwashed ones say
Arnab: You can disagree with me. But I'm not going to accept a label for having an opinion.
Gurpreet: relax, it's a joke
Arnab: Ok. I'm going to stop here for tonight. Talk tomorrow about something else?
Gurpreet: whatever
Arnab: Goodnight.

Arnab put the phone face down, heart still thudding. He did not feel like a winner. He felt like himself.

qa.q: What did Gurpreet say Arnab sounded like?
How did Arnab feel after reading Gurpreet's messages?
qa.a: He felt hurt and stung, his heart still thudding after he put the phone down.

qa.q: Which choice helped Arnab keep his dignity?
qa.a: He stated his view briefly, refused to accept the label, and ended the chat calmly instead of trying to win.

qa.q: Why might Gurpreet call the insult "a joke"?
qa.a: Gurpreet may have felt caught out by Arnab's calm reply and wanted to shrink the insult rather than admit it.

grounding: The chat shows someone dismissed as brainwashed and anti-national who states his view briefly, refuses the label and ends the talk calmly without needing to win.

passage:
At the tea stall by the bus stand in Sangli, the talk had turned to the coming election. Suraj said quietly that he thought the new canal project had been badly planned.

Rukmini, who ran the stall, snorted. "Listen to him. Two years in Pune and he comes back brainwashed. These city boys forget their own village."

The old men laughed. Suraj felt it land in his stomach. For a moment he wanted to list every report he had read.

He set his glass down. "Rukmini-akka, I grew up four houses from here. I think the canal should reach the eastern fields too. That's all."

"See? Anti-village."

"You can call it what you like. I know what I think." He counted out his coins, smiled at her, and said, "Your tea is still the best in Sangli."

He walked to the bus with his face burning and his back straight.

qa.a: Four houses from the tea stall.

qa.q: What does Suraj's burning face as he walks away suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he still felt stung and embarrassed by Rukmini's label, even though he kept his calm.

qa.q: What did Suraj get right in responding to the label?
qa.a: He stated his view in one line, refused to be defined as anti-village, and left calmly and politely instead of arguing.

qa.q: How might Rukmini see Suraj's calm answer?
qa.a: Rukmini may be a little surprised that he didn't fight back, and perhaps softened by his compliment about her tea.

grounding: The passage shows a young man dismissed as brainwashed and anti-village who states his view briefly, refuses the label and ends the exchange calmly with dignity.
